query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In pre‐exposed (passivated) Q235 steel, the originally protective passivation film degrades at high temperatures (700–900 °C) not only by mechanical spallation but also via a thermally induced compositional transformation that converts a stable, electrochemically protective layer into less adherent, non‐protective oxides. In contrast, at room temperature, the intact passivation film continues to retard corrosion by maintaining its chemical composition and barrier properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 low‐carbon steel after industrial pickling and passivation (with a dense, uniform, dark black passivation film as achieved by the standard pickling/passivation process).
generation.intervention: Subject identical batches of pre‐exposed Q235 steel to controlled thermal annealing treatments: one set maintained at room temperature and another set heated to a target regime (e.g., 700–900 °C) in a controlled salt‐containing atmosphere, with all other conditions (environment, exposure time, salt chemistry) held constant.
generation.conditions: The study is conducted under two regimes: (1) ambient conditions (room temperature, moderate humidity/salt spray) and (2) high‐temperature exposure (700–900 °C) under an aggressive salt atmosphere. The hypothesis is expected to apply to uniformly passivated Q235 steel without additional surface modifications (e.g., HEA cladding) and in environments where the high-temperature oxidation reactions are operative.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity, phase composition, and adhesion of the passivation film act as the structural mediator. Changes in the film’s microstructure (e.g., conversion of Fe2O3 or nitrite‐incorporated species to non‐protective Fe3O4 or other less adherent oxides) mediate the transition from protection to degradation.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the passivation film—with its characteristic incorporation of nitrogen, fluorine, and possibly other inhibitor residues—remains relatively stable and continuous, retarding ion transport and corrosion. At high temperatures, thermal energy accelerates diffusion and chemical reactions within the film, leading to volatilization or rearrangement of its components and conversion into a scale with high stress and poor adhesion. This transformation, in addition to any thermally induced spallation, exposes the underlying metal to rapid aggressive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature salt exposure, annealed pre-exposed Q235 samples will exhibit a measurable increase in corrosion rate (e.g., higher weight loss, more pronounced pitting, and faster kinetics in electrochemical tests) relative to unannealed, room-temperature samples. Microstructural and compositional analyses (XRD, SEM-EDS, XPS) are expected to reveal the loss of the original passivation film structure (e.g., diminished nitrogen or fluorine signals, formation of non-protective iron oxides) in high-temperature treated samples relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: Passivated Q235 steel samples maintained under room temperature salt exposure conditions, which should retain their original protective film and exhibit slower corrosion kinetics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Q235 steel in its pre-exposure (industrial passivation) state without further surface alloying or cladding modifications. It may not hold if additional stabilizing layers (e.g., high-entropy alloy coatings) are present or if the environment does not induce the same thermal oxidation reactions (such as in inert atmospheres or under less aggressive salts).
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the observation of passivation film breakdown under cyclic salt spray conditions (PMC9504384::web::009) and the temperature-accelerated passive film evolution in simulated concrete pore solutions (PMC9867134::web::023) into the high-temperature (700–900 °C) regime. It is uncertain how exactly the chemical composition (e.g., residual inhibitor elements) in the pre-passivated film will transform under these conditions, as existing high-temperature corrosion studies (e.g., PMC9100067::web::003) focus on modified surfaces. Thus, the study tests whether the same degradation mechanisms hold for unmodified, pre-exposed Q235 steel.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically passivated Q235 steel coupons. Subject one set to room temperature salt spray exposure and the other set to high-temperature (e.g., 800 °C) salt exposure for a fixed duration. Evaluate both sets using weight loss measurements, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and detailed surface characterization (XRD, SEM-EDS, XPS) to track film composition and morphology.
measurements: Weight loss and corrosion rate over time
Electrochemical impedance spectra to assess barrier properties
XRD patterns to identify oxide phases
SEM/EDS imaging to assess film morphology and adhesion
XPS to quantify changes in film elemental composition (e.g., N, F content)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature treated samples do not show significant changes in the film’s composition, morphology, or corrosion kinetics relative to room temperature samples—that is, if the protective film remains intact and the corrosion rate remains low—then the hypothesis that thermal transformation of the passivation film mediates degradation is falsified.
